content: The universal need for antiretroviral therapy (ART) among individuals living with HIV will drive the rapid expansion of ART programs. Service Delivery: Implementation Challenges and Opportunities Implementing the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and diagnostics presents several challenges, including: Selecting appropriate products. Accurately forecasting demand and quantifying needs. Managing the global supply chain to meet increasing demand. Planning and executing procurement, including timely ordering and delivery. Addressing storage and distribution constraints. Monitoring consumption and adjusting to changes in demand. Managing ARV drug pickup schedules and implementing multi-month dispensing models. Ensuring effective communication between stakeholders at all levels. Balancing costs and identifying opportunities for savings. Managing product shelf life to avoid stock-outs or expired products due to overestimation of needs. These challenges can be addressed through a national stakeholder working group that includes policymakers, implementers, funders, procurement specialists, central medical store managers, and finance ministry representatives. This group would develop a comprehensive plan to address these issues. Selection of Pharmaceutical and Diagnostic Products Medicines and diagnostic tools should align with national guidelines and programmatic needs. National guidelines must provide clear instructions for alternative regimens or diagnostic technologies in cases of drug toxicity, treatment failure, infrastructure limitations, or supply shortages, in line with WHO recommendations. WHO advises minimizing the number of ARV regimens to optimize treatment and sourcing. For example, some countries reported using over 20 ARV regimens in 2020, which complicates supply chain management. If a selected ARV drug or diagnostic is not on the national drug list or registered, HIV program managers should coordinate with the national regulatory authority to include and register these commodities. Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Testing, Treatment, and Monitoring Drugs and diagnostics no longer recommended by WHO should be removed from national ART guidelines and essential medicine lists. Plans should be made to transition patients to more effective regimens while utilizing existing stocks appropriately. Remaining stocks of outdated products should be disposed of safely. Synchronizing the introduction of new guidelines with forecasting, procurement, and distribution planning will minimize waste and shortages during the transition period. Key performance indicators should be developed to monitor drug and diagnostic use, waste, and stock-outs. Quantifying and Forecasting Demand To determine the required volume of products, procurement and supply managers need detailed information, including: The number of individuals receiving treatment, categorized by age group. The regimens being used and any proposed changes. The expected rate of treatment scale-up. The number of rapid test kits needed to meet scale-up targets. The frequency of multi-month dispensing. The approval and registration status of products in the country. For diagnostics, key information includes the number of people needing testing (e.g., CD4, infant diagnosis, viral load), the specific tests used, and the expected scale-up rate. Quantification should be conducted annually, projecting at least two years ahead, with semiannual reviews to adjust for significant changes. Assuming financial resources are available, managers can plan long-term orders with staggered delivery schedules to accommodate changes in demand and unforeseen events. Supply Planning and Procurement Procurement managers should develop a supply plan that considers: Current stock levels. Outstanding vendor orders. Available budgets for new orders. Forecasted demand, including buffer stock. Delivery timelines to prevent stock-outs. WHO recommends semiannual supply planning to adapt to demand changes and supplier delays. National procurement programs should: Consolidate procurement systems to pool ARV drug and diagnostic orders. Join pooled procurement mechanisms to access favorable prices and economies of scale. Establish long-term framework contracts for regularly demanded commodities to reduce transaction costs and delivery times. Implement multi-supplier strategies to maintain a healthy market and avoid dependence on a single supplier. Use publicly accessible databases to facilitate price transparency and competition. Storage and Distribution Proper storage and distribution of HIV medicines, diagnostics, and other commodities are critical. Countries should evaluate the appropriate levels in the supply chain to hold stock, plan for new public facilities, or consider outsourcing to private sector facilities with adequate storage capabilities. Storage and distribution plans should include: Quality assurance of products upon receipt. Secure storage facilities suitable for pharmaceuticals and diagnostics. Cold storage for temperature-sensitive products. Rationalization of storage levels to shorten the supply pipeline. Inventory control systems with appropriate reordering triggers. Regular distribution patterns to service facilities. Routine data reporting to monitor usage and adjust for changes in consumption patterns. Shelf-life management systems. Avoiding Stock-Outs and Expired Products To prevent treatment interruptions, close coordination with program managers and policymakers is necessary to align supply chain planning with treatment scale-up targets. Quantification and ordering should include a rotating safety buffer to account for forecasting errors and delivery delays. Forecasts should be revisited semiannually to adjust for variances and review demand for the next 12–18 months. Orders should be placed at least 12 months in advance to allow for production and cost-effective shipping. Staged deliveries are recommended to optimize storage and distribution capacity. Special Considerations for ART for Children Ensuring the availability of ARV formulations for children remains a challenge. WHO provides guidance on optimal ARV products for children to promote a secure and sustainable supply. National programs should transition to preferred and alternative ART regimens for infants and children as recommended by WHO. Pooling orders with other programs or countries may help address low demand for pediatric formulations. Larger buffer stocks may be necessary for essential products with low demand. Transitioning to Preferred Regimens Programs should carefully plan the transition to preferred regimens, such as dolutegravir (DTG)-based therapies, by phasing in increased quantities and liaising with suppliers to meet anticipated demand. Outdated drugs like stavudine (d4T) and nevirapine (NVP) should no longer be procured due to toxicity and lower efficacy. Patients on older regimens should be transitioned to newer, more effective options. Supply Chain Adaptations for Differentiated Care Models When implementing less frequent ARV drug pickups or community-based ART delivery, supply chain models must be agile enough to support these differentiated care approaches. Additional ARV drugs, safety buffer stocks, and enhanced reporting systems will be required to track products through community-level sites. Programs should incorporate these requirements into annual quantification, funding, and procurement plans.
